subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me start by saying I am very happy to take part in the throne speech debate. I had first intended to deal mainly with my responsibilities as Secretary of State and Minister of Communications. I decided against this because I think that we in this country are currently living critical times and that we have to tackle problems which somehow transcend our own interests, whether they be regional, provincial or other, and focus on interests and matters which have more bearing on the Canadian nation as a whole. [English]
I feel most strongly, Mr. Speaker, with the referendum staring us in the face, that my first speech in this Parliament should address itself primarily to an issue of vital interest to the nation, because notwithstanding arguments to the con-
The Address-Mr. Fox
trary, the referendum is not only a French question, not only a Quebec question, but a question affecting the future of Canada, with Quebec being an important part of that future. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the statements made by the ultra-nationalists, and particularly the separatists, indicate that they interpret the history of Quebec and that of Quebec within Canada in a way which, according to them, shows that the French language and culture have constantly been imperiled and kept from developing in our country. The conclusion drawn is that the separation of Quebec from the rest of Canada is necessary to ensure not only the respect but also the survival of French culture.
This separatist rhetoric, Mr. Speaker, is clearly fallacious. It is a fabric of lies feeding the political ambition of a group of people who merely seek total power over their fellow citizens. Mr. Speaker, the French language is alive and well as it never was before. French culture is alive and well as it never was before. To maintain that Canadian federalism has not allowed the French language and the French culture to develop and flourish within our boundaries is unfounded. It is also unfounded to maintain that Canada's central government has jeopardized the stability and the flourishing of our French fact in our Canada. In fact, the facts are quite the opposite. The facts are quite different from the separatist fiction.
Mr. Speaker, I have found in recent years, especially when meeting groups of young people in our CEGEPs, that it is always hard to explain that there is a difference between reality and fiction and to make them understand that Canada through its central government and its federal system has in fact enabled the French language to be used and to be improved in Quebec and throughout the country.
I know that some realities are hard to swallow in some separatist circles, but the fact is that they are realities. First, through its Official Languages Act, the Government of Canada acknowledged not only the historical contribution of Francophones, but also the basic role Francophones will play in the future of our country. And this has happened, Mr. Speaker, without any need to think about separation, about a break. That act had recognized, long before the Parti Quebe-cois started to move, that Canada must be bilingual and must remain so in order to be truly its own self. Progress made since the inception of that act is encouraging. That is a reality much more important than the separatist fiction.
Contrary to separatists' claim, who by the way are making entirely false statements and even distort historical facts to their advantage, Canadians know that they can communicate with the central government in the language of their choice wherever they are in Canada. They know that the Government of Canada is increasingly promoting access by all Canadians to the learning and use of the other official language and is sparing no effort to allow them to live and develop in the official language of their choice. The provincial governments

April 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Fox
also have the responsibility to ensure the development of the French-speaking community living within their territory. After many historical difficulties, some of which continue to exist, that responsibility is being increasingly recognized.
I would like, Mr. Speaker, in that respect to quote just one figure. For instance, who knows in Quebec that today in the far away province of Alberta there are as many as 75 Francophone schools? Who among the big names in the separatist movement in Quebec would tell the people of that province that today in Canada more than 203,000 children of Englishspeaking families outside Quebec are attending French immersion classes in school? This is an example of the kind of change that has occurred through the years in English Canada, in the other provinces of this great country, mention of which is very seldom made in the province of Quebec.
The members of this House know that quite well. The government of Canada encourages the teaching of the minority language in each province all across Canada. A total of $160 million has been paid by my department to the provinces for that purpose during the fiscal year 1979-80. This is a fact. To the province of Quebec alone, some $733 million, that is $300 million in direct transfers and $400 million in tax transfers, were contributed to education in 1979-80.
Who, among the staunch supporters of separatism, Mr. Speaker, has had the courage to recognize those efforts made by the central government in the field of education in the province of Quebec during the debate at the National Assembly? No one of course. But this is a fact. The young people in Quebec have more than ever before the opportunity to take advantage of new working tools, to take part in meaningful exchanges with other young Canadians, to benefit from teaching materials which help them to acquire a better command of their French and to learn English if they wish. For that purpose, an amount of $10 million, including $6 million for linguistic exchanges alone, has been paid under the Open House Canada program. That is a reality, Mr. Speaker, a verifiable fact.
The Government of Canada also helps newcomers to Quebec. It helps them to get their education in French. That is a program about which Quebec separatists keep quiet. They do not talk about the amounts spent to enable new citizens to better integrate in the Francophone life of Quebec and Canada, nor about the $11 million spent by the Department of Manpower for that purpose. Let us also mention the amounts put at the disposal of young Francophones through employment, animation and training programs such as the armed forces programs which enable young Quebeckers to get a better education in French. Quebec separatists do not talk about that either.
Mr. Speaker, I also want to mention translation programs which promote communications in both our official languages. We invest each year huge amounts in that field. Last year, for instance, the translation bureau in my department spent $50
million on its translation programs in the official languages. This amount includes $6 million for research to ensure the quality, updating and universality of the French language within our society, to set up a modern terminology bank, and link French-speaking Canada to the international data banks. Therefore, it would not be true to assert that the central government did nothing to promote the French language. Reality is quite different.
So I call upon all Quebeckers to make an honest and thorough examination because indeed, Mr. Speaker, this matter has never been examined with the intellectual honesty and earnestness it calls for. What are those realities involved? Let us take, for example, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the National Film Board, Canada Council and all the other cultural agencies of the Government of Canada; those agencies, Mr. Speaker, did not need the outbursts of the separatist government in Quebec to contribute substantially to the survival and use of the French language, and to bring about a great improvement in the quality of the French language and culture in the province of Quebec and throughout Canada.
What would the French fact be in Canada today? Would it have the same quality, the same status, the same significance if it were not for the CBC, the National Film Board, Canada Council, the National Museums, Public Archives and all the other agencies of the central government? Again, those are realities, not illusions, not talk, but facts, real facts, true facts. No honest citizen, can pretend that Radio-Canada has not been in the past and does not continue to be a major catalyser of the most dynamic elements in the Francophone information, and artistic communities, which enabled them to achieve success and growth. It would now be opportune to make a few comments about the quality of the French language, which Radio-Canada announcers have been displaying for many years. From Henri Bergeron to Rene Lecavalier, all announcers have always promoted high standards for the French, not the English language, not the promotion of "joual", but the promotion of good French. That is a fact.
I could also quote figures in this connection. Let us take for example the year 1977-78. Radio-Canada spent over $200 million in the province of Quebec, that is 36 per cent of its over-all expenditures in that same year. That is much more than the strict mathematical percentage that is so dear to the Pequistes, a strict mathematical percentage based on population. That year the corporation employed 4,300 persons in Quebec. Is that really a federal government that tries to hinder French culture? The salaries of those employees and related expenses total more than $100 million. The total value of Radio-Canada's capital investments in the province of Quebec as of March 31, 1978, amounted to $151 million. That also is a fact.
April 17, 1980

How many of our artists have benefited some time or other from Radio-Canada? How many of our cultural or even social and political groups have come to be known through Radio-Canada? And that situation prevails since the very beginning of TV in Canada. It did not wait for separatist agitation.
I could also speak of the National Film Board, Mr. Speaker. Let us ask our Quebec separatists where our Quebec filmmakers, our Francophone filmmakers, would stand without the National Film Board. We could point out that the Government of Canada, and the National Film Board, have within a federal Canada given an opportunity for all our talents to come of age; for Claude Jutras to create Mon oncle Antoine, for Gilles Carle, Jean-Pierre Lefebvre, Pierre Perrault and so many others to express their creativity.
And what about the new tax measures giving a new boost to the Francophone film industry in Canada? That is also a fact. The Government of Canada does not lay any conditions for its support of Francophone creative talents and cultural instruments. It does not impose any political censorship. It does not urge artists to become members of a particular committee rather than another. To my knowledge, Radio-Canada has never been known to be teeming with federalists.

speechtext:
This real freedom is also a fact. Do we really find the same freedom in all the interventions of the Parti Quebe-cois government on linguistic and cultural matters? Is there really the same quality of freedom and the same opportunities to express different views within some agencies of the Parti Quebecois government? Have we heard many federalists over Radio-Quebec? We must think about that too, Mr. Speaker.
I could also say much more about Canada Council. Once again, reality is far from separatist fiction. It is the opposite of the false statements that are rammed down the people's throats under the guise of nice songs and high-falutin elucidations. Where would all our creative talents, all our artists, all our craftsmen, all our drama groups, all our musical and dance organizations be without the support of Canada Council and Radio-Canada? The Government of Canada has for several decades been the mainstay of artistic creation and the major prop of Francophone artistic development. Once again, this is a fact. This is a fact that hurts in some circles, but that is one we must not overlook.
I would like, Mr. Speaker, to address for a few moments the most creative minds of our society. Where would we be today if, at a time when the government of Quebec was not much concerned with culture, information or university education, when some public figures derided what they termed "artistic art", the Government of Canada had not been there and if a federal system of government had not been able to compensate-and I emphasize compensate-for a lack of understanding in some responsible quarters. Those things did happen in the past and they are true. Those are facts. How could anyone now argue that the Government of Canada has tried to overshadow the French fact, to make French-speaking artists
The Address-Mr. Fox
subservient to the English-speaking majority whereas what really happened is exactly the opposite? How could we reasonably claim that artistic creation would be stimulated if Quebec were to secede? Those issues require more pondering over.
Furthermore, in a sovereign Quebec in which the Parti Quebecois is committed to maintain all social transfer payments, pay the salaries of former federal employees and many other expenditures, what would be the working margin, what resources would be left for the government to support artistic and cultural activities? This is a question we must now ask ourselves and answer without delay.
Those are the facts we must face now. Under the guise of lovely songs which are sometimes I quite agree very beautiful and displays of passion probably, the big guns of the Parti Quebecois go around distorting reality, disguising facts, spreading lies which if repeated often enough will finally be accepted as truths. They ask the people to trade their birthright for a mess of pottage, to trade the positive support of the Government of Canada which is a concrete reality for a would-be society of which the only indisputable feature is the fact that a small elitist group would gain absolute power over the people of Quebec.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, at this political turning point in our history, on the eve of the Quebec referendum, 1 would like to deal with two other matters which are of particular interest to me.
Personally, I have always been irritated by the way the separatist speakers seem to enjoy confusing the issues. And such confusion which has been deliberately spread around for a number of years must be dispelled. I am referring to the fact that they confuse the problems that may confront the Frenchspeaking community with the problems that may confront Quebeckers as citizens of a particular region. How can anyone go on suggesting that all of Quebec's problems are due to the fact that there is in our country an English-speaking majority and a French-speaking minority?
A very large number of the existing problems are regional, social and economic problems that have nothing to do with the French nature of Quebec. A very large part of Quebec's problems are caused by social, geographic or economic conditions that have nothing to do with le fait fran^ais as such. It is dishonest to have people believe that all the existing problems in Quebec have as their one and only cause the strained relationship between the two linguistic communities.
Unemployment problems in some areas, the problem of industrial development in Quebec for example, are based on geographic and economic data and having nothing to do with the French fact. It seems to me that it should no longer be possible to make the people believe that all those problems would disappear immediately after Quebec achieved sovereignty-

April 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Fox
However, we all know very well that the separatist star performers are spreading all those dreams. The liberation of everyone is now connected to a so-called liberation of Quebec. There is some confusion there between a certain type of problem related to the linguistic make-up of our country and another type of problem related to geographic and economic data, and this confusion should not be ignored any longer.
This leads me, Mr. Speaker, to another aspect of the debate which deserves close attention. Preserving the French language and culture, setting up the framework and the tools to guarantee their dynamic development are not the game preserves of the separatists. They are dear to the hearts of all Quebeckers, whether they toil in the private or public sectors, whether they toil in Ottawa or in Quebec. The will to remain French is every bit as strong among federalists who work with the central government as among the separatists who work in the National Assembly. To claim the contrary is dishonest.
There certainly have been moments of tension in our Canadian history. Those moments must neither be downplayed nor exaggerated. But they cannot be expected to disappear some day. Tensions are part of life itself. They would even exist in a system born of a type of sovereignty-association. But just as it has been done in the course of the last decades and as it will always be necessary to continue doing so, every means must be taken to make both linguistic groups in our country understand the positive contribution of the other, the need to fully respect it and appreciate its differences.
Those past incidents which often go far back in our history have been such, and I readily agree, that no Francophone wants to leave his linguistic fate entirely in the hands of the other linguistic group of the country. This political will is a basic political fact in our country. But this political will, Mr. Speaker, does not necessarily require going from a federal to a unitary system, from a Canada with two co-existing linguistic communities to a separate Quebec state.
We find, Mr. Speaker, that in Mr. Camille Laurin's white paper, an anthropological method is used to interpret society. In that white paper, the linguistic phenomenon is referred to as a basic feature of daily life in Quebec around which are centred all other aspects of life and which serves to interpret the remainder of the community. All the vital manifestations of a community are subjected to the language criterion alone.
The anthropological method is an interesting interpretation tool. But it is far from being as relevant as some would suggest or as effective in the daily life of every citizen of our province. Every Quebecker understands that there are other factors in his life besides the linguistic one, that there are, among others, political, social, economic, ethnic, religous factors. It is true that there are English-speaking Canadians on the one hand and French-speaking Canadians on the other, but it is equally true that there are a great many other factors which differentiate amongst our fellow-citizens and which, in fact, unite Canadians much more than they divide them. There are many more elements which unite the citizens of our country than
elements which divide them. What unites us is much stronger than what makes us different. What we have in common is more important than what sets us apart.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to go over this same argument differently. For me, in my political philosophy, in my view of the political organization of the country and society, in my conception of the instruments needed by a society to ensure its development, I am completely opposed to any kind of exclusive jurisdiction and control. I am all the more opposed to such control as this type of society which some are trying to sell us would destroy one of the best means we have had throughout our history to develop and to ensure as much as possible that individual rights are respected. I cannot accept that a single government could have complete control over my life, over the legislation which affects me, over my taxes. On the contrary, I believe that it is healthy, especially in the areas which affect our everyday life, which affect the fabric of our society, which affect culture, for no government to have complete control over what concerns us. I believe it is healthy that there should be some competition between two levels of government to better protect the rights of citizens.
Mr. Speaker, the debate on Quebec separation has been going on for several years. A majority of citizens are still dead set against the projects of the separatists, that of sovereignty. In fact, this relentless opposition has been understood even by the Parti Quebecois. At the present time, the referendum debate does not deal with the separation project because it would be categorically rejected by the population. But they are still trying to bring Quebeckers gradually to take one more step in a direction they reject. There is dishonesty in the gradual approach being proposed by the Parti Quebecois. There seems to me to be a basic lack of respect for the people of Quebec. They seem to me to be trying to do indirectly and gradually what the people do not want to do directly and clearly.
The present referendum debate still remains a historical debate that will be an essential element in the evolution of all citizens of Quebec as well as that of all other citizens of Canada. That historical debate has led the separatists of the Parti Quebecois to make totally false assertions. It is false to pretend that Quebec needs a Yes to secure a mandate to get things moving when, quite to the contrary, the reality is that the mandate to get things moving is on the No side. It is false that Quebec must separate to ensure the maintenance and the development of the French language and culture in Quebec itself. Contrary to what they say in separatist circles, the Government of Canada, both in the past and in the present-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank my colleagues. In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I must say that contrary to what separatists have been saying for a long time, the Government of Canada, both in the past and in the present, and it will be the same in the future, has been an all essential and privileged instrument to promote the development of the quality of the French language and culture. That French fact which is recognized today not only at home but all over the world would not be as vigorous, as rich, as promising had it not been for the whole positive contribution of the Government of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the federal system of our Canada is a much better instrument to ensure the progress of French and the promotion of Francophones than a Unitarian system would be, a political system that would isolate Quebeckers from the real challenges, the challenges of a universe in which people who are different will have to have learned to live together to ensure peace, freedom, security and prosperity for all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my constituency of Bruce-Grey I welcome the opportunity to join in the response to the Speech from the Throne which has opened this Thirty-second Parliament.
First, may I congratulate Madam Speaker on her appointment as Speaker and wish her a successful term. Second, I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his colleagues on their successful campaign. I wish them well in their deliberations on behalf of this country.
In my initial speech in this House I would like to exercise the privilege of referring to my constituency of Bruce-Grey. One of the most unique aspects of this constituency is treasures which are hidden within its boundaries: from the caves of the islands off Tobermory, down the beautiful Niagara escarpment and Georgian Bay and along the shoreline of unspoiled Lake Huron, from the awesome Bruce nuclear power development and its surrounding Scottish communities to the industrious Hanover which forms the heartland of a thriving furniture industry, and from the German community of Neustadt to the resilient Durham, and beyond this to the security and stability of Walter's Falls; they are treasures in themselves and all enclosing a productive rural community.
This riding should be identified as a breeding ground for some great politicians, at least until now. The Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker was born in Neustadt, and the great-grandfather of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) homesteaded in Kincardine township. Its basic resource in people, however, is in those who have remained in the farming communities, which continue to thrive. This human resource has recently been augmented by people who have come in numbers to the area to build and operate what is to be the largest nuclear complex in the world.
The Address-Mr. Gurbin
The natural attributes have allowed many of our citizens to work in the tourist trade, while others find employment in a variety of manufacturing industries but particularly in furniture and wood products.
The main issues which are important to the people I am here to represent are really not much different from the basic concerns which exist across my province of Ontario and throughout our whole country.
Beef and other farming activities in Bruce-Grey are among the most productive in Canada. Farming through our independent farming operations is to our future what oil and energy resources are to today. Unfortunately, in the throne speech we have failed to take any meaningful initiatives to allow farming operations to continue their economic survival.
Worst of all, because of debt and costs, this year some cannot afford to sow their crops unless they sell capital investments. Some will not plant. The individual economic hardships farmers face are serious enough; the loss of productive farm capacity in a world of hunger is tragic. This problem has a good deal to do with the prices farmers are able to get for their products. I applaud the proposed expansion of export markets through a Canadian agricultural export corporation. I am encouraged by the indication of meat import legislation and hope that it will be an effective instrument for beef producers. I hope that the election promise of a farm price review will in fact happen. I sincerely hope that this government will provide some short-term relief for the survival of our farmers until economic conditions improve.
Nuclear energy has had a very emotional and uneven history. It has developed in the shadow of the most destructive force yet devised by man, and in the wake of Three Mile Island this shadow has almost eclipsed the entire American nuclear program. Our nuclear resources in Canada have developed on the basis of need, particularly in the industrial heartland of Canada, in Ontario.
Bruce-Grey has in progress the second major phase of a construction program which will provide approximately one quarter of all the electrical energy in Ontario. This complex, based on the prize of Canadian technology, the Candu system, will also provide the largest steam plant in the world and enough steam to run four of Alberta's syncrude plants.
This complex also gives the largest North American example of the combined use of an energy source to produce both electricity and steam energy for industrial activity. The heavy water plants use massive amounts of steam to produce heavy water for our Candu system.
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for the digression, but the explanation was important both in terms of the indication in the throne speech to create an alternative energy corporation and also in the critical energy future of Ontario.

April 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Gurbin
Amazing economic opportunities could result from the full utilization of the energy facilities now in place. Improvement of fuel efficiency from less than one third to more than two thirds is an exciting potential. The combination of this efficiency improvement with the existing technologies of portable fuels, including methanol, ethanol and hydrogen, give Ontario an energy future which can be capable of significant independence. I believe we could have energy self-reliance for Ontario by the year 2000.
An additional comment is appropriate in discussing this energy future. The integration of the conservation of cogenerated heat units combined with biomass from trees or other cellulose sources, cash crops starch sources, sugar sources or from waste products, forms a cycle to produce a hydrocarbon from a renewable source.
The nuclear component of this combination presents to Ontario an opportunity to achieve a degree of independence and remain competitive with those provinces which are endowed with fossil fuel deposits or massive hydroelectric opportunities. In addition, significant reductions in carbon dioxide emissions can occur. This can help avoid the so-called atmospheric greenhouse effect.
An important element in the ongoing Canadian energy discussion is the provincial constitutional control of energy resources. This dialogue can be assisted by the understanding in Ontario of the potential we have.
In our own area we have in process now the development of a particular expression of cogeneration. This expression is in the form of a small greenhouse prototype which is one acre in size. This prototype in fact is developed using three different types of greenhouse structure, and at the present time it is in the middle of its second crop of producing cucumbers and tomatoes for the markets of Ontario and Canada.
In developing this technique and producing this variety of greenhouse produce we expose to Canada a technology that can be used to develop a marketable produce from our own energy resource. We can in fact replace imports which are coming in at the rate of approximately $200 million a year, and we can do this with an energy source that is now in place.
In the throne speech there is one item which gives me cause for concern, and this is the projection of Canadian ownership of our petroleum industry to the extent of 50 per cent by the year 1990. I do not understand how this can occur unless we are talking about nationalization. I do not understand how we can in fact achieve 50 per cent Canadian ownership without massive government involvement. I think that the government must be more clear in designating how this is to occur and what technique will be used.
Tourism is an ongoing important source of revenue and it is also a source of employment in Bruce-Grey as in many other areas of Canada. Tourism can be seen to be neglected by the Speech from the Throne. My hope would be that we will give more attention to this in the coming months. A specific national tourist policy and specific initiatives to help the
industry develop could help local economies and Canada's balance of trade deficits.
Railways and mass transportation systems of the last decade are inadequate for present needs. It is encouraging to note a recognition of this in the throne speech, but little comfort is seen in the lack of specific planning except for the wheat transportation improvements already initiated by the last government. The deterioration of facilities almost guarantees continued loss of current rail services. I believe a review process, the so-called rationalization of rail services, that is taking place now for the first time in Canada in our own area should provide an excellent prototype for the development of a national, economically-viable, integrated rail system. This integration of systems would allow the use of freight, rail and tourism lines combined together to provide an economically viable unit.
I think it is important that the members of this House remember, while we debate the Speech from the Throne, that the impact of our deliberations will not be felt today but by future generations of Canadians. Therefore, we have an obligation to ensure that our decisions are not based upon selfishness but upon an honest regard for the needs and aspirations of our children.
Governments too often place themselves in positions of serving the desires of today by ransoming the future. Social programs are instituted, non-renewable resources are consumed and new laws are created with a flagrant disregard for the effects that such decisions will have upon the quality of life of our descendants. As representatives of the people, we must keep vigil over their interests. We must attempt to protect the rights not only of the majority, but also those of groups unable to stand in self-defence. Such a group is the young.
The young are eager to prove themselves. They want to get out in the world and establish their credibility. This is a task which is becoming increasingly difficult. No longer is an education enough to get a secure and well-paying job; no longer is a home within the means of most young Canadians; no longer can the young look forward to the standard of living that we promised them.
What promise does this throne speech, this government, hold out to the young? Oh, yes, I see a reference to creating new jobs. But what does this mean? Does it mean a new opportunities for youth program? If so, it will not be of much use to Bruce-Grey or, for that matter, many other parts of the country. We need permanent, meaningful employment, not band-aids. We need protection from interest rates so that young people will be able to continue the family farm or business. We need new industry and new jobs based not upon the wishes of a bureaucracy, but upon the real needs and the vast potential of our country. We need to put an end to inflation so that once again young people will feel secure enough to be able to own a home and raise a family.
We need to re-examine the educational system and the role it plays in preparing young Canadians for what lies ahead. This may mean an increased concentration on skills training, but it definitely means that access to education must be
April 17, 1980

affordable. We need to be able to assure the young that we have taken adequate precaution to preserve a secure source of energy for the future. We need to come to terms with our environment in such a way as to protect valuable farm land and vacation areas from the challenges posed by pollution, and thus save these resources for our future needs.
But most of all we need to be able to convince the young that they have a government which is committed to looking out for their interests. This implies a government which is willing to set an example, a government which is willing to provide some standards by which the young may judge themselves. In short, it requires a government which understands the needs of Canada and is willing to respond with vigour and determination.
While providing for the economic well-being of the nation, the government must also prove that it has an understanding of laws that give a country its spirit. It must be willing to enforce those laws which are just and should change those which are not.
If I could be allowed to digress again for a moment, the government must be able to understand the need for capital punishment as well as a tightening of the abortion laws. I have yet to be convinced that the government is capable of that level of understanding. For example, the government has stated its intent to decriminalize simple possession of cannabis. I would hope that the government would place careful consideration into the framing of such legislation. I for one do not believe that the government should take any steps which might lead Canadians to believe that this Elouse supports the use of marijuana. On the other hand, it is important that young people not be faced with the spectre of a criminal record for experimenting with a habit which has received tacit approval from certain sectors of our society.
Cannabis serves as an excellent example of a policy area where a decision made today could have serious detrimental effects upon our country a few years down the road. Recent information more and more points to the likelihood of cannabis being dangerous to one's health. Just as we must worry about the dangerous effects of giving young men and women criminal records, we must also worry about the dangerous effects of the widespread use of drugs. The government will not receive my support for any piece of legislation that does not include substantial penalties for those who traffic in drugs.

Furthermore, I believe it essential that the government ensures that a program of drug education is instituted to teach young Canadians about the possible effects of marijuana use.
Today our Canadian family is faced with a predictable circumstance. As dependencies between the Canadian parent and the provincial offspring have changed with time, so too the formal relationships of these must be re-established. Fate, as a father, has typically wandered off to thrust his proverbial finger in other directions. As a mother, Canada has an historical and geographical bonding with her provincial children that
The Address-Mr. Pinard
will withstand politics, economics and even temporary insanity so long as our borders are secure from external forces. Even as we continue our constitutional and referendum debate, the failure to recognize the extraterritorial threat handicaps us, because by recognizing it fully the crisis could help reaffirm the bonding and secure our family unit.
By not recognizing the Russian military and political expansion for what it is, we contribute to the increased isolation and vulnerability of our provinces and our country. The purchase of new fighter aircraft and a recommitment to our full part in NATO is a hopeful indication that this government recognizes the threat, and in the face of this crisis will do its part to secure peace and a continuation of confederation.
I thank Mr. Speaker and my colleagues for the opportunity of joining them in this debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier today during the question period one of my colleagues asked me a question to which of course 1 gave the best possible reply under the circumstances, but I would have liked to be much more precise. The colleague who put the question is a federal member from the province of Quebec who seemed concerned about the time available to him to play effectively his role as a legislator in the Canadian Parliament while supporting those who are fighting for a united Canada in the present referendum debate in Quebec.
My colleague was wondering whether as government leader in the House and as President of the Privy Council I could not assure him that he would have the necessary time to discharge the double task entrusted to him. And I have every reason to believe that since he was chairman of the Quebec caucus in Ottawa he was speaking for most if not all of his colleagues. I replied that of course our mandate will be practically double during the coming days and weeks. Double in the sense that first we have a mandate and a duty to govern this country and at the same time we have to get involved and help our brothers and sisters in Quebec who do not want to abandon Canada and are anxious to fight for building a strong and united Canada. It is in that context that I had to reply that I would have to co-operate with the official opposition and the New Democratic Party and rely on their co-operation.
The aspect on which I would like to dwell at the outset of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, is that of course all hon. members wish for a majority of No votes in the referendum which will be held on May 20 next and of course all hon. members would like to contribute directly or indirectly to that victory for Canada. I would respectfully suggest that one way of contributing even indirectly would be to allow the proceedings in the House in the weeks to come, as an example for the future,

April 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Pinard
to get on in the most complete harmony among all parties without denying the right and privilege of the opposition parties to criticize government measures thoroughly but not dilatorily.
Today 1 call upon the sense of responsibility of the opposition parties so that we and all members of the House who so desire can, in the next few weeks, organize rationally their work schedule and devote all their time and energy to not only governing the country, which of course is essential, but also to defending the cause of Canada and of Quebeckers who want to stay in Canada, in their country, in the province of Quebec.
I am sure that my colleagues will give me their full co-operation, and I refer specifically to the House leaders of the two opposition parties. 1 am sure that they are aware of the very positive role they can play in the present debate, not by relinquishing their right, as opposition parties, to criticize government legislation, but by showing as much flexibility and co-operation as possible to allow us parliamentarians from Quebec especially to meet both objectives and fulfil both roles so that we can help govern Canada and work towards its unity.
Mr. Speaker, I entered politics for a very simple reason. It was not for a question of boundaries, but for the economic and social well-being of the region I come from. 1 entered politics to improve the social and economic conditions of my province and also of my country, Canada. When 1 first ran, in 1974, in the riding where I was born, a region based on the textile industry, a region, I would say, of average economic growth rate, my objective was, and that is the expression 1 used, to go into public life in the hope of trying to make people smile. My objective was to try and make the people from my region, my province, my country happier. It is as simple as that. In the present debate, in the referendum debate, it is in that spirit that I will deal with the question that is asked of my fellow citizens, both men and women, from Quebec.
It seems that since the debate on the referendum question in the National Assembly, a large number of my fellow citizens in the province of Quebec are somehow hypnotized by glib, pompous speakers, albeit short on logic.
The danger is that during. that debate in the National Assembly when the referendum question was supposed to be discussed, they dealt with everything except the question itself. And as a member from an area where 99 per cent of the people are ordinary people, in the coming days and the coming weeks I want very much the debate to be brought down to their level so that they may understand. I would like the debate that the Pequistes have been conducting at the level of academics to be stopped so that the people in Quebec may be told very simply: Well, we have a question to put to you, this is the question, and that is where the answer we want will lead you. And what is happening now is that all sorts of gratuitous assertions are being made, as mentioned by previous speakers, assertions which are not based on facts, are often misleading and have the effect of hypnotizing my fellow citizens, as I said
earlier. So what I want to do today actually is to warn my fellow citizens against what is going on now and prompt them to give much thought to the matter, if they are asked a question, to analyse its content and take into consideration who is asking it.
In my riding of Drummond, Mr. Speaker, there are textile workers, workers in small and medium-sized business and industrial milk producers. That is fairly characteristic of several areas in the province of Quebec. They are hard-working people. They are people for whom bread and butter issues, economic issues are vital in that debate. And it is very important that they know that a Yes or No can have serious consequences and repercussions on their lives after the May 20 referendum.
So I ask those people to consider two things: first, and it is normal, someone is asking you a question that you will have to answer on May 20. We should ask ourselves first who asked the question, because before we give an answer, it is always important to know who asked for something, and for what? We can appreciate the answer is very simple but we must be careful because it is an important question; and it is also important to know who asks the question, it is a question of credibility. The question is asked by the government of the Parti Quebecois. The question has been prepared and adopted by the majority of a political party, a party whose program is seeking very clearly the independence of Quebec. So, in the beginning, it is important to indicate to all those ordinary people that someone wants an answer, they want a Yes from you. Those people are members of a political party in Quebec which is dedicated to the separation and independence of Quebec. That is the primary reason to be careful, to be fully aware of the fact that the Parti Quebecois refused to really debate the question at the National Assembly a few weeks ago. What is really the question being asked by politicians of the Parti Quebecois who want Quebec to be independent? Well, let us have a look at the wording of the question. We will not likely be mistaken if we look at the second paragraph of that long question, and I quote:
That agreement will allow Quebec to gain exclusive power to pass its legislation, to collect its taxes and to establish its foreign relations, which is sovereignty and at the same time, association.
The question is crystal clear, Mr. Speaker. The Parti Quebecois wants a Yes for a mandate to negotiate sovereignty, which is synonymous with independence and separation. So the ordinary people from my riding, who work for average wages and who, when unemployed because of difficult economic times, avail themselves of the very generous unemployment insurance plan we have developed in this country, those same people who, when sick, benefit from medical and hospital care or, when aged, receive old age security pensions, these same people have the right to ask themselves: the political party which is asking me this question wants to say Yes to the independence of Quebec, that political party wants me to give
April 17, 1980

it a mandate to negotiate the separation of the province of Quebec and at the same time achieve economic association, an impossibility in itself, considering what the provincial premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada have said, namely that sovereignty was not negotiable and that we did not have the mandate to negotiate it.
The important thing is to say to these people: Listen, the Parti Quebecois is asking you to agree to a mandate to negotiate Quebec independence. If you are asked to say Yes to this question, you are entitled to demand that they prove clearly that following this mandate, you will live in economic and social conditions at least as good as those which now prevail. Mr. Speaker, the burden of proof lies with those who want to break up a country to attempt to create another one.
It is up to the Parti Quebecois to show the ordinary citizens of Quebec and to all Quebeckers that once this mandate is obtained, these people will be as well off as they are now. The question I am asking it is a legitimate one. The Parti Quebecois supporters are the ones who want to change the order of things, they are the ones who want to change federalism for an independent Quebec in the more or less short term, and it is up to them to prove conclusively that if they obtain this mandate, the ordinary citizens whom they seem to want to exploit by calling unduly on a so-called pride will be able to live in conditions at least as good as those they now enjoy. God knows that this proof is far from made.
We are now living, as we are well aware, in a province, and a country, which have virtually the most advanced social legislation in the world.
We live in a rich country, and those who want to change the order of things, the political status of part of this country, should at least have the decency to show clearly to Quebec citizens that they will enjoy at least the same economic and social advantages as those for which I have been fighting since my arrival on the political scene. However, Mr. Speaker, I am not so sure that they will have the honesty to debate the issue at this level. Mr. Speaker, I shall come back to those whom I represent more particularly because I know them well. Let us talk about the textile workers. They are well aware that in the last few years the Canadian government has succeeded in negotiating bilateral agreements with seven, eight, or nine southeastern Asia countries to limit imports of clothing manufactured at a lower cost to allow our textile industry to be more competitive and more efficient.
These quotas were imposed by the then minister of industry, trade and commerce (Mr. Chretien) and were renewed last year, that is quite recently, for three years and even five in some cases. The simple fact of limiting clothing imports forces citizens in other parts of Canada to pay more for their clothes. It is obvious that if fewer shirts made in Hong Kong reach our market, British Columbia or Alberta citizens will have to purchase a shirt made in Canada which will cost more than if it came from Hong Kong.
The Address-Mr. Pinard
Mr. Speaker, we now have Canadian men and women who are willing to pay more for their clothes because they agree to some degree to protect our textile industry. And by protecting our Canadian textile industry to some degree we are protecting those jobs. There is another way in which the government protects our textile and clothing industry to some degree, because that protection is always limited, and this is the GATT and its agreements on tariffs and quotas on textile and fibre imports.
When we put together those two Canadian policies, the result of sound federalism, we see that our Canadian textile industry is able to fare better, perform better, and as a consequence prevent the erosion of its workers' standard of living and job security in general. This way we can save hundreds if not thousands of jobs in the Canadian textile and clothing industry in Canada, thanks to our sound Canadian policies in that area. Those policies have been implemented and made possible because Canada was powerful enough to reach bilateral agreements, as I said, with seven, eight or nine countries, and also achieve favourable results at the Geneva talks under the GATT.
What I am asking from the Pequistes who are soliciting a Yes vote which means a mandate to separate Quebec from Canada, is that they prove, since the burden of proof is on them, to the textile workers in my constituency of Drummond, and everywhere in Quebec, that the morning after their mandate there will not be such insecurity that Canadians will not feel inclined to put pressure on the government to be able to buy their clothes cheaper, and that the morning after Quebec is sovereign we will enjoy similar protection for the textile industry which accounts for the majority of jobs in the province of Quebec. This is my first question to them.
I would also like to ask them to prove to my voters, to my textile workers, just how, in the wake of Quebec sovereignty, independence or separation since that is what it is called, there could be as many jobs and as sound health standards as there are now, for these are due, chiefly, to federal policies in this sector.
About 15 years ago the textile industry employed 45 per cent of all the industrial manpower in my area. At this very moment, it hardly employs 8 per cent of active manpower in the riding of Drummond. What has happened in the meantime? A department which was created here in Ottawa in 1969, the Department of Regional and Economic Expansion, tries to redress regional inequalities and it had a very positive impact on areas such as the one 1 represent. This, Mr. Chairman, is another positive aspect of our brand of federalism. By injecting capital supplied by this Department, we were able to diversify our industry and see to it that jobs in the textile sector which were doomed to disappear because of the modernization of the industry could be transferred to newly created small and medium-sized businesses.

April 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Pinard
In fact, millions of dollars were spent in the riding of Drummond alone by the Department of Regional and Economic Expansion in an effort to help us achieve this industrial diversification and to provide jobs to our Quebec fellow citizens living in that area. This is another advantage which the Parti Quebecois is duty-bound to mention. It must prove to my fellow citizens in that Drummond riding that the same diversification would be possible in a separate independent Quebec. I am not saying that it will not be done up to a certain point. I ask them to do their duty, because it is up to them to prove it during the referendum campaign. This is what the people want to know. They want to know whether on the first day of sovereignty they will hold the same jobs and get the same social benefits.
Will we have the same freedom, will we be as secure as we are now after having agreed to give the Quebec government the mandate to negotiate sovereignty-association? This question is quite legitimate, Mr. Speaker. It is essential that the Parti Quebecois give the ordinary people in Quebec the proof they ask for and stop spreading these half-truths or untruths in some cases in order to hypnotize the population and take undue advantage of a false sense of pride.
Our approach in this debate is noble, Mr. Speaker. What we say is that it is much more courageous and much more generous to take up the challenge of diversity. Canada has its two founding peoples. Certainly injustice has been committed in the past and I have already indicated in the House that we should not react with frustration and egoism as the PQ would have us do. History should teach us a lesson of generosity and courage.
Our ancestors, Mr. Speaker, have worked hard in this country to give us the wealth we have from one ocean to the other. Our children have the right to insist that we do not take a decision which will deprive them of that wealth they are entitled to. In this country, Mr. Speaker, we have the opportunity to meet a challenge, to go forth on what the Prime Minister often calls the road of excellence and to fight here in Ottawa in order that our two founding peoples may live in harmony and full equality. The fact is that there are many Francophones sitting here in this Parliament.
There are 16 French-speaking members of the cabinet out of 31 or 32. That is a little better than the equality talked about by the Parti Quebecois. What the people are asked in the referendum is for the exclusive right to make laws. They are told: "People of Quebec, you made a mistake last February 18. Some 68 per cent of all of you have sent men and women to Ottawa to make laws, to represent you, to try and bring harmony and development in the strictest equality of a strong and united Canada; you clearly and massively asked those people to act as your representatives, precisely to make laws. Now we tell you to forget that and give us an exclusive
mandate to make laws here in Quebec." I think it is ridiculous, Mr. Speaker, and that it is to play a bad joke on people and not respect them to ask them, after they have given their massive support to men and women who are now members of Parliament from Quebec in Ottawa, and proud to be Canadians, for an answer that negates the intentions expressed by the people of Quebec a few weeks ago. That is something the ordinary people should easily understand.
The attitude of the Parti Quebecois toward the injustices I mentioned-this may seem a paradox since they are asking for a Yes vote-is a very negative one. They say: Well, listen, there is nothing else we can do about it, the solution is territorial withdrawal. Let us abandon to their fate a few hundred thousand French-speaking people outside Quebec, let us leave them to their fate, we are going to work it out for ourselves in Quebec, we will make our own laws, we will collect our own taxes. Of course this is not practically feasible without an economic association. However, people know very well that this economic association accompanying sovereignty is not negotiable, that answering Yes to this question would lead Quebec in an absolute dead-end, a cul-de-sac. The result of this dead-end will not be the constitutional changes so greatly hoped for, it will not be a renewed federalism, the result will quite simply be yet more uncertainty, harmful to the economy of this country and particularly to the economy of the province of Quebec. That is another aspect which must be pointed out in this debate.
Mr. Speaker, as it has been said many times over, one can be both a good Quebecker and a good Canadian. I was born in the area I represent and when, over the weekend, with my fellow members of the No committee I launched its campaign in my riding, I said that my soul belonged to Drummondville and my heart to Quebec, but that body and soul I was a Canadian. It is in that spirit that today, as simply as possible, I ask of my fellow citizens of the riding I represent, that when the time comes for them to answer the question which basically constitutes one step towards the independence of Quebec, they reflect seriously upon the element of pride inherent in the gesture that is generous, that is constructive, the gesture which really tries to avoid barriers and boundaries in our society, that we might seek to live in harmony, in as sound and just an economy as possible.
It seems to me that when the time comes to answer that question, the people will have to ask themselves whether the PQ government has proved that, should it be given the mandate to negotiate for every part of the province of Quebec, its citizens will have at least the same advantages they now have. Should the mandate to negotiate be granted, should the Yes have it, will we be proud of having sulked about past injustices, of having followed the examples set by those who were frustrated by history and who preach territorial withdrawal instead of having the courage to build a strong and united Canada under the most flexible system in the world which can
April 17, 1980

function perfectly only when its members, men and women alike, really want to negotiate and talk to each other.
Mr. Speaker, I can give you more that one example of what I have just asserted. Mr. Levesque already has the mandate to negotiate the best terms possible for the people of Quebec: he has it now. When twice he slammed doors in our faces here in Ottawa during federal-provincial conferences, he had the mandate to improve the economic and social conditions of the citizens of Quebec. In fact, that is the mandate he was given when he was elected: give Quebec a good government. But instead of negotiating, he came here with the deliberate intention of proving that no success was possible in negotiations with the Canadian government and the governments of the other provinces. He is a slave to the program of his party, he must achieve the independence of Quebec and his strategy is very simple: slam doors here in Ottawa and implement the good recommendations of his chief advisor "Pere Gedeon", that is, achieve independence on the QT.
And that, Mr. Speaker, is what Quebec people must know. With his referendum, Mr. Levesque is putting into action a carefully planned strategy whereby twice he would slam doors here on the economic and social development of Quebec and Canada, and now, claiming his so-called pride to be a Quebecker, he is asking a mandate to come and negotiate the impossible. And then he would be able to return to the men and women in Quebec and say: "You see, they refuse to negotiate sovereignty-association. So, give us the authority to separate." He will have achieved what he set out to do and he will have completed his carefully planned strategy. People must be made aware of this.
People must consider this question in the context of the PQ election in 1976 up to the independence of Quebec which is part of the PQ platform. And this question is nothing more than a step toward the independence of Quebec. And I say to my fellow Canadians that we can be proud to be Canadians, to vote No to such a question, to work in a Canada where we feel fine as Quebeckers, to live as I do in Drummondville and to follow the road of excellence and courage rather than the path of defeatism and separation from a country and wealth which belong to us and our children.

Mr. Speaker, I heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) say "There cheers for Nova Scotia". It is nice to have the kind of ally he has been for Nova Scotians during the period that he and I have served together in the House of Commons.
This is a rather different Parliament for me from any of the nine previous in which I have served, different because the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker is no longer with us. While he did not sit in the last Parliament he was elected to it, and he added much indeed to the folklore of this nation from every
The Address-Mr. Coates
point of view, much to the history of Canada, much to the commitment as one individual to one Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, from the 49th parallel to the Arctic, and much to make Canada a better place for all of us to live. I miss him very much and I am sure that there are many other Canadians like me who miss him a great deal, especially in troubled times like these when we could always look upon him as a great champion for the people of Canada regardless from where they came, regardless of their ethnic extraction, regardless of their role in life. Whether they be the high and mighty or the lowly, he was their friend, their champion. He was special.

speechtext:
Today, Canadians almost appear determined to involve themselves in a form of constitutional masochism, whether it be Quebec separatism or western alienation, rather than accepting the God-given advantages that almost make us the mother-lode of this planet.
At a time when the world is broadening its horizons, when new economic and political unions are binding areas of the earth together, when these new unions are cutting through narrow nationalistic ties, without threatening those nationalistic bonds and achieving significant economic benefits, it seems almost impossible to conceive that we would consider marching down a road that could ultimately destroy this confederation.
We now know that the agony of the present debate in Quebec on the specific matter of sovereignty-association- whatever that means-will end on May 20. In view of the fact that the issue seems little more than an operation in frustra-
126

April 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Coates
tion, since all of Quebec's partners have indicated no willingness to discuss the matter after May 20, what is to be gained by Quebec or the nation is beyond my comprehension. 1 wish my colleagues in this House my very best wishes as they put forward the many sound and sensible reasons for maintaining this union that has been of such tremendous benefit to all in this nation and comparatively provides so much more to those who live here than is possible almost anywhere else in the world.
And yet with all of this evidence marshalled on the side of retaining our confederation, it seems that everywhere one goes in Canada today and from what we read and hear in the media leads one to conclude that the most common feeling or perception is that Canadians are puzzled, apprehensive and nervous about the future. A sense of malaise is widely prevalent across the land.
How can we account for this widespread feeling of malaise and apprehension? 1 do not profess to be any great analyst of the condition of modern society. I do not understand the jargon and many of the concepts that some of the so-called analysts use. Sometimes I wonder if they do so themselves, but 1 think having been re-elected successfully ten times to this House, having served as president of my party and having known and worked with a great many politicians over 23 years, I think this gives me some credentials to answer the basic question which is being asked more and more these days at home and abroad: "What seems to have gone wrong with Canada?".
It may well be that our thoughts have centred on our own deficiencies because we have been involved almost totally in the electoral process since. 1978. It is often said that one cannot see the forest for the trees. We have not been looking at what has been actually happening in the world, although we know with the energy crisis that has been upon us since the early 1970s that OPEC, by using the vehicle of an international economic union, has caused havoc with the financial viability of the industrialized world.
With the EEC we have witnessed, once again, that the economic clout of Europe has been enhanced without any real erosion, feared by many, occurring to the participating nations.
We hear a great deal of the economic nationalism that frightens many because of what they perceive to be the economic domination of our industrial base by the multinational corporations that are mainly based in the United States. What we do not seem to want to face up to is the fact that Canadians are traders and have proven over our 113-year history to be good traders. Indeed, the people from my province were expert traders long before there was a Canada, and indeed provided a success story prior to confederation that has not been equalled since 1867.
If we are to enjoy the benefits that match our potential we must look outward, not inward. We must look at the total North American continent, Canada, the United States and Mexico, and decide how as the people of this continent we can harness the possibilities that exist.
Let me say that I welcome the forthcoming visit of the President of Mexico and hope his visit will provide a productive opportunity for some discussions about the many common interests we share with that great nation. Mexico has come alive as a vital and vibrant nation in the new economic order. It, like Canada, sits on the border of the economic giant of the free world. It, like Canada, must face up to the identity problem that comes from being a neighbour of this great nation.
But neither Canada nor Mexico can achieve anything but benefits from charting a course that takes advantage of the possibilities that accrue from the fact that 220 million or more people in the United States provide a market, close at hand, with fewer obstacles than exist anywhere else on earth.
Let me just stress a few realities. Our economic relationship with the United States is overwhelming. Our Canadian investment patterns are showing a strong thrust into the U.S.; more and more Canadians are buying properties in the U.S.; and on all the big issues in the world our interest and those of the Americans are identical.
We are currently wrestling with the issue of the Olympic boycott. Our citizens feel as the Clark government felt when we stated we would also support that boycott. We are now awaiting the decision of the Trudeau government. I would feel a deep sense of betrayal for our best friend if our positions were to be anything other than the positive one taken by the Clark government.
We are indeed fortunate to have as the United States ambassador to Canada the hon. Kenneth Curtis. Ken Curtis has a history of a lifetime of close association with Canada. When governor of the state of Maine, he spearheaded the development of a formalized association between the governors of the New England states and the five eastern provinces of Canada. He later assumed heavy obligations within his own political party, the Democratic party, as chairman of their organization.
We then have in Canada today a man of significant ability, one who knows Canada well and knows the United States and its political institutions in a way not available to most in that nation, and who has already displayed a special and unique style of diplomacy in international affairs in our midst. What better man could be found to help us embark upon a new initiative in North American relations?
1 have been impressed with the amount of activity of a positive nature that has been developing in recent years regarding closer arrangements between Canada and the United States. 1 refer to the Canadian Senate and especially its standing committee on foreign affairs. That committee produced a most helpful report on Canada's trade relationship with the United States. There are also the reports of the C. D. Howe Research Institute and reports of the sub-committee of the United States Senate chaired by Senator Baucus.
But one of the most imaginative suggestions I have seen comes from a former adviser to my leader, Mr. Duncan
April 17, 1980

Edmonds, who has developed proposals that could lead to a treaty of North America. Mr. Edmonds has established himself as a significant person in the political, academic and business community, as a man of great foresight in national and international affairs. His production of a draft treaty approach among Canada, the United States and Mexico provides the catalyst for the type of discussion that can only be of value and benefit for all who live on the North American continent. Mr. Edmonds' provocative proposals have recently been published in a number of Canadian newspapers across Canada, as well as being reprinted in the congressional record. 1 believe that Mr. Edmonds' analysis and suggestions for a closer structured relationship with the United States and Mexico would benefit all three countries and would certainly work to greatly strengthen Canada.
I would like to draw to the attention of the House some very interesting developments which have been stimulated by the national governors' association of the United States. That body today, comprised of the governors of all 50 states of the United States, has recently passed a detailed resolution earlier this year, from which 1 quote:
Finally and most importantly, the federal government is encouraged to explore the possibility of immediate trilateral discussions concerning the establishment of an appropriate forum for discovering potential areas of future co-operation. Such a forum whether achieved through existing or newly created channels, should:
1)	Guarantee the integrity and interest of each country;
2)	Ensure that areas identified for study and discussion are agreed upon by full consensus;
3)	Provide for equal representation for each country;
4)	Ensure, in addition to federal participation, adequate representation from state and provincial governments, local governments and the private sector; and
5)	Reserve actual policy decisions to the sovereign discretion of each country.
The chairman of the international trade committee of the national governors' association, governor Busbee of Georgia, has in co-operation with the Dean Rusk Centre at the University of Georgia produced some very excellent material,including a very major fact book and a very substantive memorandum on how we might proceed to get a greater degree of co-operation between Canada and the United States. I recommend that those who believe there is the type of merit 1 see in such future initiatives look closely at the proposal from the Dean Rusk Centre for the establishment of a North American council. Quoting from their report of November 16, 1979, on North American co-operation, they state on page 12:
The centrepiece of the proposed National Governors' Association initiatives is a trilateral framework organization, which will serve as the most visible manifestation of the willingness of all three countries to solve continental problems through a continental approach, while ensuring the participation of those parties most actively involved in North American affairs.
As is generally the case with framework organizations, the North American council would be primarily consultative in nature, with most of its work carried out in the normal activities of its membership. During the initial phase at least, plenary sessions of the council would be utilized to flesh out the commitment of Canada, Mexico, and the U.S. to a trilateral decision-making approach, establish personal contacts among the representatives, and set up a system for communications to ensure the continuation of council work in the interim period. This work can be further defined-and concrete responsibility assigned-by setting up specialized committees (trilateral) and subcommittees (either bilateral or concerned with specific projects) with authority to make findings of fact and
The Address-Mr. Mackasey
recommendations to the council as a whole. Committee and subcommittee members could be left to make mutually convenient arrangements for meetings, timetables, and internal distribution of responsibility. The proposed trilateral communications system will provide the main forum for committee work. The major purpose of the council is to inculcate the habit of trilateral thinking among the decision-making elites of North America. Establishment of full-time representatives-or even a full-time staff, beyond the minimum necessary for administration-would be self-defeating, since the council is designed to reach persons who may spend only a portion of their time in foreign relations matters.
The National Governors' Association can take the initiative in establishing a North American Council and thereby assure itself a leading role in all subsequent trilateral endeavours. With this end in mind, the following steps are recommended:
(1)	NGA should appoint regional committees to contact public and private parties involved in trade or other contacts with Canada and Mexico, to "talk up'' the project, solicit ideas, and obtain pledges of participation and support;
(2)	NGA may then select a number of governors (representing each region) most interested in the project as its delegation to the council;
(3)	Federal authorities should be contacted and a representative group of federal policymakers co-opted to the delegation;
(4)	The delegation should be filled out with business leaders, academicians, and local officials, with the paramount criteria being a position of influence affecting relations with Canada or Mexico and at least general support for the project as a whole;
(5)	NGA should then sponsor a "call" to appropriate institutions in Canada and Mexico for the selection from each country of a delegation equal in number to that chosen by NGA; stipulated as principles for selection should be diversity in both geography and function, experience and authority in North American affairs, and inclusion of private interests.
I believe that there is enormous potential in these developments. In my judgment, the working out of a new set of arrangements with the United States and Mexico will be the dominant question of the 1980s. I commend this material to the House and suggest that it is the area where we can finally rediscover a sense of direction for Canada.
As Sir John A. Macdonald said over a century ago, geography is destiny; and as we move into the 1980s we are very fortunate to live beside the United States and to have an opportunity to work out with them and the Mexicans a closer set of relationships. The new set of relationships should strengthen Canada and should allow us to retain our sovereignty and independence while continuing to make a significant contribution to the world at large.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude by reiterating Mr. Edmonds' conclusion in his own proposal:
We have an opportunity to manage the process where history is inexorably taking us anyway. Rarely do a people have the opportunity we have now as Canadians to seize the moment where we are faced with a great national uncertainty and a sense of malaise and to replace that with a dynamic new sense of ourselves in partnership with the whole North American continent. We ought to begin this great task immediately.
