speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, through you, I wish to congratulate Madam Speaker on her election. I am sure that she will carry out with distinction the duties of the post that you share tonight, and add that grace which is so much a part of her person. Acting as the first woman Speaker of the House of Commons in Canada is but a continuation of her past accomplishments in her many fields of interest in Canada and on the international scene.
I am proud to be here as the representative of Edmonton South which is part of a growing city full of promise for the future. This year marks the seventy-fifth anniversary of the province of Alberta, and 1 hope many Canadians will have the opportunity to visit our province as well as the city of Edmonton and experience for themselves the spirit of growth and adventure that characterizes our community.
I thank my electors for having shown confidence in me for the fourth time, and I hope that I will be able to merit the continuation of that confidence.
Canada is engulfed in a crisis of staggering proportions. Not in our lifetime have the combined economic, energy and political problems of Canada been greater than at this moment. The country is reeling under unprecedented interest rates, intolerable government, debt and ceaseless inflation. Polls indicate that the separatist voices could win the Quebec referendum, which would be the bitterest blow to confederation in our 113 years.
A new government, elected with virtually no support west of Winnipeg, has already twice given the back of its hand to western Canada on the essential questions of energy and transportation. Is it any wonder that the air is filled with anger, and anger that 1 personally experienced at a town hall meeting I called for my constituents in Edmonton South after the election? People seek order and they are given chaos. They want stability and they are given drift. They want leadership and they are given politics. It is a moment for all of us who want a united Canada with economic strength and renewed federalism, to stand up. If we who want to build on the legacy that we have received do not speak out to protect Canada, the Canada that we love, then the forces of those who would separate and destroy the country will surely grow.
1 appeal to members on all sides of the House. 1 say let us together repair the terrible divisions in this land.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I say let us through this institution provide the economic, social and political leadership Canadians so desperately seek today. Let us unite-at least in this analysis-that a Yes vote in the referendum will tear Canada apart irreparably, for western Canada will never tolerate a government rejected by westerners at the polls and which, in turn, is rejected by the very province that the government depends upon for electoral support.
The Address-Mr. Roche
We must abandon sophisticated interpretations of the referendum question. I know that it is deviously worded, but, outside Quebec, Yes will mean that Quebec wants out, and when that happens Canada will explode.
As an Albertan my appeal to the people of Quebec is to vote No in the referendum. A No vote is not a vote for the status quo, for the western provinces also want a renewed federalism, one which would reflect the new position of the west in confederation, a renewed confederation, and which would also provide Quebec with an acceptable alternative to separation.
My work has taken me into every corner of the world. 1 know how blessed our land is with space, resources, technology, industry, and an environment that promotes a quality of life second to none in the world. We cannot fail to be proud of our country. It is all the more reason to be angry over the problems that beset us, that keep us bogged down, constantly turned inward when we should be raising our heads looking out into the world that needs the leadership and production that Canada can offer.
The problems of Canada are not insoluble, but they require more political honesty, more belt-tightening, and a greater sense of justice than they now receive. Like Quebec the west is frustrated by the current federal system which has failed to respond adequately to the changing conditions within Canada today. Western frustration is rooted more in economics than in culture as Albertans see the money that they provide through equalization payments, income taxes, oil and gas revenues going to a government which is more attentive to the large electorally strong consumer centre of Canada than to the sparsely populated regional resource regions.
The separatist movement which has grown out of the seeds of discontent is not yet strong in western Canada, but the potential is there if the federal government is not responsive to western concerns that have been elaborated for many years by western members that I see surrounding me tonight in the House.
A recent poll taken by people at the Edmonton Journal and The Calgary Herald shows that 68 per cent of Albertans feel that their interests are not being adequately represented in Ottawa. What does that tell us? It tells us that the west is waiting for clear signs of this government's commitment. So far the signs have not been hopeful. I listened carefully two days ago when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made his speech. I have to say in all honesty that I felt the Prime Minister again dismissed the problems of regional fair treatment too casually. The decision by the federal government to use the emergency provisions of the oil sands pricing agreement to put a ceiling on the price of synthetic crude oil has disrupted the industry and cast doubts upon the intentions of the federal government in the oil-pricing negotiations with Alberta. The Alberta government has already reacted strongly against the move, and the future of the two oil sands plants is in jeopardy because of the industry's lack of confidence in federal government agreements.

April 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Roche
I plead with members on the other side of the House to think about these problems for they are every bit as much at the heart of the question of unity in our country as is the Quebec referendum. The refusal by the federal government to commit itself to the Conservative government's agreement to provide $30 million for infrastructure costs at the proposed Prince Rupert grain terminal has also jeopardized western reactions to this government. It has certainly jeopardized the future of grain transportation in our country.
There have been other moves by the government seen as discriminatory in the west. For example, the reduction in private utilities federal income tax rebates to the provinces affects Alberta more than any other province and has been felt directly by many Albertans through increased utility costs. It is a needless thing for the government to do.
The sincerity of the government's commitment to the west can be tested in several ways. An energy pricing agreement should be concluded with Alberta that provides no less benefits than would have been received as a result of negotiations with the Clark government. The producing provinces must be compensated fairly for their rapidly depleting resources. That is the essence of the Alberta position today. We heard it conveyed by Premier Lougheed to the Canadian Press dinner last night in Toronto. I want to tell my colleagues in the House that the people of Alberta are 100 per cent behind Lougheed as he defends the Alberta position nationally.
Transportation policies are needed for both goods and people, policies that recognize the essential role played by transportation in the continued development of the west. Grievances persist in the area over the adverse effect of the Crowsnest Pass rates on producers of finished goods in the west, over the irrationality of the grain transportation system, over the destruction of railway communities caused by rail line abandonment. The time for action is now if serious economic repercussions in the west are to be avoided.
Westerners also want industrial development policies which will provide more incentive to manufacturers to locate in the west. Agriculture and livestock policies should ensure a more equitable and stabilized return for western farmers. These are some of the things that are fundamental to our position as we come into the House to start a new Parliament.
We give a commitment to renewed federalism. We want to see the government move forward in those concrete steps that show a sincere concern for the interests of western Canada. Our constitution has proven remarkably adaptable in the years of our confederation, but I think we are pretty well all agreed that it needs to be changed. It is no longer appropriate for today's reality. That is the essence of the Quebec position.
Renewed federalism through constitutional amendment should reflect the desire of the regions to respond effectively to the needs of their people while maintaining a united Canada under a strong central government.

Any proposals for change to the federal system will have to take into account the views of the west. The Alberta government has already outlined its proposals in its paper called "Harmony and Diversity" which is designed to encourage national unity as well as effective operation of the federal system. The paper suggests that the division of powers be modified to strengthen provincial ownership and control of natural resources, provide provincial access to direct and indirect taxes, and establish concurrent jurisdiction in the fields of communication, fisheries, transportation and culture. The federal ability to act in provincial jurisdictions would be restricted to well-defined limits. The principle of equalization would be entrenched in the constitution and French and English recognized as Canada's official languages.
The Quebec Liberal party's document "A New Canadian Federation", the Ryan beige paper, offers a rational and comprehensive analysis of our current dilemma. That paper is worthy of support. I personally have some disagreement with some aspects of the Ryan paper, but it is at least dedicated to the fundamental principles of equality of the two founding peoples and respect for regional and cultural diversity principles that Canadians share today.
There are differences in the various proposals and papers put forward, whether they are talking about the Canada West foundation, the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce, the city of Edmonton, the Pepin-Robarts report that we discussed in the Parliament before last; all of these share the same basic objectives of a strong and united Canada where we are willing to negotiate compromises. This willingness to negotiate will help to ensure that the central government is not weakened to the point of ineffectiveness in the face of economic and social problems that require a strong national response.
A renewed federalism will enable all regions of Canada to develop to their fullest potential and take advantage of the opportunities that this country has to offer, opportunities that we could not spend enough time exploring and exposing in this House for all Canadians who are reading and seeing us here, for them to appreciate as much as we who have the opportunity of travelling regularly across this country.
We need sound economic and energy policies. That is part of our struggle for national unity. We should recall the sentence given in the speech by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in his contribution to this debate two days ago when he said:
-the importance of the referendum is no excuse for delaying action on economic policy, no excuse for delaying action on energy policy and no excuse for avoiding our international obligations. Indeed, delay in dealing with those acute problems may very well aggravate the tensions which now exist in the Canadian family.
Severe economic problems are controlling the country rather than the other way around. Despite their strong and vibrant economy, Albertans are concerned about the trends in other regions of Canada. Our strength depends on the strength of these regions, and we look to the federal government to take action in its sphere of influence.
Alberta would like to see less government influence over the economy and more reliance on the private sector. Government
April 17, 1980

waste and mismanagement have to be curbed, and a climate of confidence created for investment in our country. This requires an answer to the problems of high interest rates, inflation, and government debt, and a comprehensive industrial development strategy. Alberta is willing to make its contribution, and in fact already forgoes S4 billion in oil and gas revenues each year. Loans have been provided through the Heritage Fund to six other provinces, helping Canada's balance of payments by lowering interest payments outside of the country. And the Alberta government is willing to increase the amount available for provincial loans.
These remarks tonight would not be complete if we just dealt with economic problems. I want to talk for a minute about social problems. Just as we should not be diverted from our economic problems by the national unity problem, we should not allow these two problems to divert our attention from the deep social problems in our midst today. The powerful tide of change which is sweeping across the world today is tearing our families apart, rocking our economy, paralysing our political systems, shattering our values, while at the same time paradoxically sowing the seeds for a saner, wiser and more humane society. For more on this I would refer you to Alvin Toffler's "The Third Wave". It is an interesting analysis of the changes that are taking place in the world today.
What we must learn from this process is that development in our supertechnological society should focus on values of humanism, on values of the person, not just on values of the economy. We must encompass our natural environment, social relations, education. Those are the questions that are concerning Canadians very much tonight.
We in this House must ask ourselves, as this Parliament proceeds, some very hard questions about the quality of life in our society today. Why have crime, violence, divorce, suicide, abortions, drug abuse, and alcoholism soared in the last decade? In 1978, 140,000 Canadians were victims of violent crimes. Divorce rates have doubled in the last decade. More than one in four marriages in Canada ends in divorce. Suicide is the number two cause of death among 15 to 34 year olds. It is not my purpose here tonight to assign blame regarding these very complicated and meaningful statistics, but only to indicate to this House the ethical crisis that we face in the midst of a growing economy. Politicians cannot solve these problems alone; we are the first to know that. But I think there must be more leadership from all levels of government today concerning the deep social problems in our midst.
We must ask why there are so many poor among us in our society? Some 24 per cent of Canadian families lack the financial means to ensure the basic necessities of adequate food, clothing and shelter. Three-quarters of our elderly are living on incomes of less than $5,000 a year. The struggle by native people to share in the benefits of our life continues. This is a point I have argued on several occasions in the time I have been in this House, namely, the need to integrate more closely economic and social planning on behalf of human beings who, after all, are the object of our policies, not just national statistics. With a strong and united Canada dedicated to the
The Address-Mr. Roche
economic and social well-being of its citizens and the citizens of other countries, I think our country would be able to exercise a more vigorous role in the international community. I conclude, Mr. Speaker, with a few remarks in that area.
A declaration of support for the boycott of the Moscow Olympics would today be a clear sign of leadership in the international community.

By delaying that decision the government is merely weakening the effectiveness of the response. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan has been condemned by the world community. A boycott of the Olympics is the strongest indication of our condemnation that we can deliver to the people of the Soviet Union without entering into military action. So why do we not take this initiative now? The people of Canada are looking to us in this House to give them some leadership in response to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. In the past Canadian foreign policy has been diverted from longer term interests by short-term economic problems and goals.
Another publication that I commend to members of this House is the Brandt commission report. The Brandt commission has been studying for two years the whole problem of North-South relations. It is the finest single document you can put your hands on today, putting into perspective the problems of and the solutions to the north-south dilemma-the dilemma of the rich and poor nations of the world. It is called, "North-South: A Program for Survival," and it outlines the magnitude of the changes and the multidimensional dangers and unprecedented opportunities we now face in a world which is changing rapidly before Our eyes.
A new way of thinking is required to turn our mutual interests with developing countries into creative partnerships- partnerships which would increase the chances of achieving global stability and security, and meet the human needs of the world's peoples. This is an opportunity and an obligation for Canada. Canada needs to develop an integrated policy in response to changing conditions in the world. Such a policy would include trade investment, aid and immigration objectives. The UN special session on international development strategy for the beginning of the third development decade is fast approaching. What is the policy of the government toward it? What thinking is being done to advance a realistic, sensible approach for Canada in the North-South role? A start, Mr. Speaker, would certainly be a parliamentary review of foreign policy. Our party has been advocating this for some time. We believe that in the ten years since foreign policy has been totally reviewed in our country, so many things have happened-it would take a whole speech in itself to outline all the things that happened in the 1970s-to make a further review necessary and that the government would be well advised to move in this area.
I applaud the government decision to establish an ambassador for disarmament. The arms race poses the greatest

April 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Simmons
immediate threat to world security, and a strong Canadian initiative should be welcome. An ambassador will help to put the spotlight on disarmament and mobilize public opinion behind the necessity to attack this very real problem. We face a dilemma here. Security is a two-sided coin. Just as we must maintain our commitment to NATO and play our role militarily in contributing to the defence of the western world, so at the same time we must work through the UN agencies to control the arms race. This seems to some people to be a contradictory position but it is only a reflection of the paradox of our age. If we are to make the world a safer place, these are the steps which must be taken by the government.
The response of the government to the plight of the IndoChinese refugees and Cubans seeking asylum in the Peruvian embassy is also to be applauded.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I think that in this Parliament we should look for action in the ways the directors of the United Church suggested in their letter to the Prime Minister which was published just a day or two ago, a very important letter that I commend to all members of the House. With what degree of urgency and priority will your government act to remedy current injustices at home and overseas? How will the official welcome sound to refugees needing Canadian asylum; to native peoples with their land claims; to pensioners pauperized by inflation; to the unemployed and unemployable; to home owners ousted by record interest levels; and to the growing numbers concerned that Canada cannot continue indefinitely in social peace and prosperity without greater economic independence?

In a most eloquent manner he spelled out for us the very essence of this confederation and the urgent justification for its continuance, though, of course, in a renewed form which recognizes present day realities and requirements.
I was not born a Canadian. My fatherland was the dominion of Newfoundland which was a sovereign state for over a hundred years until 1949 when it joined confederation. I still remember the campaign in favour of Newfoundland's joining confederation as well as the referenda. I recall the anxiety, the bitterness and the fear of the day. My father who is now 75, though he voted in favour of confederation, still considers himself a Newfoundlander first but takes pride in being a Canadian. My father as well as many other persons in Newfoundland who remember the events that preceded 1949 have discovered that it is possible to be both a Newfoundlander and a Canadian. And I will tell you why.
April 17, 1980

[ Translation]
When Newfoundland became part of our confederation, we did not relinquish, suppress or liquidate our sovereignty. On the contrary, we increased it, we put it to work in order to steer our aspirations towards economic and cultural freedom. We have indeed succeeded.
Freedom is an empty word if you have no market on which to sell your goods, if you have no employment, if you run the risk of losing your heritage, your culture because you are overly concerned by personal financial hardships. Our culture and our heritage are precious to us Newfoundlanders, and today we are witnessing a thriving period that we did not experience in the forties and all of that was made possible because we are now part of Canada.
In Newfoundland and Labrador, our culture and economic freedom have flourished remarkably since 1949, and that, because of confederation. Ours is the only Canadian province which negotiated its union with Canada during this century. Despite everything, after an alliance of 31 years, we believe that union must be improved. So, we are not surprised that the people of Quebec, one of the founding provinces of confederation, should ask that a closer look be taken of the terms of confederation after 113 years. There is not a single province in Canada which would agree to confederation continuing as it exists today. All political parties in this House have expressed publicly their wish to see confederation improved, renewed. And our Prime Minister has indicated to us that he and his government not only agree but are eager to work towards that end.
There is not a province anywhere in this country, be it one of the western provinces, to which reference was made a moment ago, Quebec, my own province of Newfoundland and Labrador, or any other, which should be content to have the Canadian confederation existing in its present form. On that I believe, partisanship aside, either in this House or across the country, we are all very much agreed. As the Prime Minister said on Tuesday and on many occasions before, we in this government are ready to get on with the job. That is why a Yes result in the Quebec referendum is unthinkable. It is unthinkable both in terms of Quebec's interests, in the interests of Newfoundland and Labrador, and in the interests of every province and of every Canadian.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to appeal to my fellow countrymen in the province of Quebec to record a resounding No vote on May 20 because that is the only vote which will launch, not only Quebec but my province, this nation and all of us, on the road to renewed and better federalism. Thank you.

It is my hope to convey to this House this evening the feelings of my fellow Albertans, and particularly the feelings of my constituents in Calgary South as they relate to national unity. The people of Calgary South are very concerned about the Quebec referendum and about the possibility that Quebeckers may choose to separate from the rest of Canada. The people of Calgary South earnestly hope that our country will stay together.

I will not presume to speak of the concerns of the Quebeckers in the national unity debate, other than to say that my constituents have no sympathy for the argument of sovereignty-association. It is equally important for Quebeckers to know that Albertans pray with all their hearts that Quebeckers will find it within their hearts to stay within confederation. Albertans are deeply concerned for the future of Canada. They are frustrated and discouraged with their federal government, but they are loyal to Canada and they want to resolve those frustrations within the context of confederation. There is very little support for the idea of western Canadian separation.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his speech stated that disagreement among the members of this House should not be based on regional interests, but should be based on the concept of the whole which we are trying to serve in different ways. I am certain that each member of this House is trying to serve Canada no less than he.
There is no argument, I believe, in this House that this House must represent the national will and the national interest. But, Mr. Speaker, if I do not represent the regional aspirations of Alberta and of my constituents in Calgary South as those aspirations relate to the matters governed by federal jurisdiction, who will represent those interests?
In our present federal electoral system it certainly would be unreasonable for me to accept the view that the two most populated provinces of Canada by themselves represent the national will or the national interest.
The Prime Minister talked of patriotism and the feeling of belonging to and of loving a country. I believe that every Canadian deeply loves Canada in his own way, even if he expresses it differently than his fellow Canadians.
I spoke of the frustration which exists in Alberta today. In Calgary South these concerns, frustrations and even hostility are expressed very openly almost every day. What puzzles me, and what puzzles other Albertans, is the lack of understanding by eastern Canadians of the spirit and the potential of western Canada. We have failed to get through to eastern Canada.
The Prime Minister has stated on a number of occasions that he does not understand the west, and this is evident, unfortunately, by his government's statements and actions

April 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Thomson
which seemingly are designed to antagonize the people of western Canada deliberately. Let me give two recent examples of this antagonism. They are with respect to the Prince Rupert terminal facility which has been spoken about in this House on numerous occasions, and the reneging of the oil sands pricing agreement. It may well be that the oil sands pricing agreement should be changed. Maybe Syncrude and Suncor should not receive escalating world prices, but the point I want to make is that these decisions were made unilaterally by the federal government without the slightest consultation. In the case of the oil sands pricing agreement, does consultation mean a telephone call one hour before it is announced to the press? Is that consultation?
Metrication and federal intrusions into housing and medicare are other examples of policies which have alienated western Canadians, just to name a few. The domestic oil price freeze of 1973, and numerous government interventions in the oil and gas industry are seen by westerners as discrimination against their interests. Albertans, particularly those from the generations preceding me, have enormous pride in Canada. I am not trying to suggest that their pride is any greater than that of the gentleman from Newfoundland or members from the other provinces of this country. All I am trying to say is that people of Alberta have a feeling of belonging to something that they have built themselves with very little help from the rest of Canada. These are self-made men and women who have developed self-reliance. They are entrepreneurs and are fiercely independent. They resent deeply the heavy hand of government.
The farmers and cattle raising communities in Alberta are bitter because of the lack of help they received during the hard times of the 1920s and 1930s when there was no, or very little, market for their produce, and the droughts of those years destroyed many of their crops. These people feel that they were left to fend for themselves during the years of the depression with precious little assistance from the central government.
During recent years transportation and terminal facilities have failed to keep pace with western Canadian grain production. Tariff and freight rates have consistently discriminated against western Canada. Albertans feel that they have been ignored, and now, when western Canadians are enjoying prosperity from their natural resources and agriculture, they feel that the central government and eastern Canada are trying to steal something away from them for which they have worked very hard. They feel that the rules of the game have been changed in mid stream.
There is also the firm belief that westerners have been unfairly called upon to pay world prices for eastern manufactured goods which are protected by tariffs while, at the same time, they are being asked to sell their resources and their crops at less than world value. Since 1947 when the Leduc oil field was discovered, Alberta has moved ahead in giant steps, largely because of the strength of its oil and gas industry. I
was fortunate enough to be a part of this economic development, and I can say that eastern investors would not help to finance this development and that the oil and gas exploration industry was forced to turn to the United States for investment. Again this is one of a number of reasons for the feeling of hostility which expresses itself today in Alberta. Is it small wonder that the oil and gas industry is owned to such a high degree by foreigners?
It is ironic that this ownership is resented by many economic nationalists today, and yet without those foreign investors we would not enjoy the benefits that we do today from the oil and gas resources of western Canada. I think that is ironic, considering that we have today in the country a feeling of economic nationalism. It is also a mystery to me why the Speech from the Throne indicates the intention of the government to buy back foreign ownership when Canada is facing a crucial shortage of needed capital to help it achieve energy self-sufficiency.
Does the Liberal government or, for that matter, does anyone really believe that Canada really has the necessary resources in this country to finance energy self-sufficiency? No, my friends, we do not have it. And to lead the Canadian people to believe that we do is false. Many easterners think that Alberta is greedy and is being unreasonable in its demands with respect to oil and gas pricing. The oil and gas resources of Alberta are being depleted quickly. Over the next ten years our production capability will be reduced by more than one half. Alberta has a very short time to diversify its economy so that future generations may enjoy the same prosperity that we do today. Our production will be reduced by one-half in ten years' time. I am not exaggerating. Those are known facts as stated by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. They are well known to members on all sides of the House.
Alberta is not, and has not been, inflexible with respect to the pricing of its oil and gas, as some people would have us believe. The province of Alberta has made an unparalleled subsidy to the rest of Canada in terms of the difference between the world price for oil and that being charged to Canadians. The sum total of this subsidy since 1973 has been in the order of $15 billion. The agreement which was reached between the Conservative government and the province of Alberta would have provided further subsidies to Canadians totalling almost $20 billion over the next five years.
There are a few other points on the energy issue which I would like to draw to the attention of members of the House that relate specifically to the oil prices. The federal minister of energy made reference in his speech yesterday to the fact that the former Conservative government would have let OPEC determine Canadian oil prices. That statement is not true, Mr. Speaker. The agreement reached by our government would have ultimately tied Canadian oil prices to 85 per cent of the composite price for oil in the United States. This is usually referred to as the Chicago composite price. It bears no relationship whatsoever to the OPEC price today, nor would it in
April 17, 1980

the future. The minister went on to say that the federal government loses when OPEC gains. The reason for this is quite simple. It is due to the fact that under the Liberal energy policy established in 1975 they chose to subsidize Canadian consumers for the difference between the cost of imported oil and the domestic oil price. In short, the Liberal government chose to deficit finance the cost of this subsidy. That is why the federal government is losing when OPEC gains.
The Liberal government deliberately chose to pass on the debt that was being incurred as the result of the difference between imported oil and the domestic oil price to future generations of Canadians. Our government, the Conservative government, believed that Canadians should face up to the reality of the cost of imported oil and that this cost should be borne by Canadians who are using that oil today, and not by our children.
Another point with respect to OPEC oil prices which I think many Canadians misunderstand is that they believe that OPEC oil prices are still being determined by a cartel and that this price bears no relation to fair market value.

POST OFFICE-RURAL SATURDAY POST OFFICE SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) for the answers he gave me this morning about the postal service.

I was pleased to hear the minister say this morning that he does not wish to cut back Saturday postal service in the rural areas. I was pleased to hear him say that this is also the present Liberal government's policy. Many of my colleagues and I have received numerous representations protesting the proposals of the previous Conservative government.
Let me mention at the outset several reasons why the people of my constituency found the Conservative proposals unacceptable. In my constituency I have some 34 municipalities as well
Adjournment Debate
as many unincorporated villages and village communities which would be affected if there were any reduction in Saturday postal service.
First of all, before I proceed I should like to thank my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker), our postal critic, who encouraged me to raise my constituents' concerns regarding their postal service.
The postal service in my constituency is a vital public service, Mr. Speaker. The postal service must be looked at as the hub of a wheel, not as a mere spoke in a wheel. The Saturday postal service is an economic hub in the rural village wheel. If the post office were closed on Saturdays the rural residents would drive to the nearest city where there is a sub post office. They would do all their shopping there, to the detriment of the smaller village. The removal of money from a village also means the removal of jobs.
Weekly newspapers would also be hit. Many newspapers in my riding publish in the latter part of the week. If the newspapers did not make Friday delivery, they would not reach their destination until Monday. Hence, all the advertising functions are lost, hurting the small businessmen who want to capitalize on the day many people come to town.
The postal service in rural constituencies is also a political hub in the rural wheel. For many rural citizens the post office is the only link with the federal government. They see the post office as more than a place for stamps and mail; the post office is the place to pick up income tax forms, passport forms, and information on government programs.
I should also like to argue that the post offices are a social hub in the rural way of life. Postmasters in my constituency are community leaders. They are dedicated to their tasks. They believe in service to the public. They provide a personal service that cannot be found in larger, more impersonal urban centres. Saturday, for the postmasters, is one of their busiest days.
In the February 15, 1980, issue of the Journal the previous postmaster general was reported as saying that he was studying the idea of closing post offices on Saturdays in order to save money. In fact the previous government has closed Pembroke and Peterborough on an experimental basis. The response to the previous government's suggestions can be illustrated by some of the representations I received from my constituency. Specifically, for example, Mr. Drebinsky, the secretary-treasurer of the rural municipality of Gilbert Plains, writes as follows:
The reeve and council of the rural municipality of Gilbert Plains strongly object to the proposal. It may be fine in larger towns and cities. But it will only further reduce the business in smaller communities if Saturday closing is implemented.
He goes on to say:
There must be other means of reducing Canada Post costs. Please pass on our objections to the higher authorities in the best way possible.
Similarly, Mr. Speaker, the mayor and council of the village of Gilbert Plains have passed the following resolution:

April 17, 1980
Adjournment Debate
Whereas current plans of the Canada Post are to implement a Saturday closing of postal services in all small communities in Canada;
And whereas the council of the village of Gilbert Plains deems this action to be detrimental to the economic welfare of the community and is of the opinion that such actions will adversely affect the survival of all small communities;
And whereas the council of the village of Gilbert Plains is of the opinion that all services cannot be equated with dollars as is the apparent suggestion of Canada Post;
Therefore be it resolved that we petition our local representatives to both the provincial and federal governments to intervene and stop the actions of Canada Post which are so detrimental to the well-being of small communities such as ours.
Likewise, Mr. Speaker, the reeve and the council of the rural municipality of Ochre River have passed a resolution which reads:
Whereas closing of the post office on Saturdays will impose a severe problem towards smaller communities, both towards businesses and mail service to customers;
And whereas a move in this direction will further speed up closing of smaller communities as well as movement out of the surrounding country;
Therefore be it resolved that we strongly protest against the closing of the post office on Saturdays.
The secretary-treasurer of the village of Minitonas, Mr. Bruce, writes on behalf of that northern village in my constituency:
The opportunity to have mail service available in the small communities is vital to the economy of the community. I cannot estimate the numbers of persons who come to towns Saturday to get mail. Likely an accurate figure would not be available. The important fact is, however, while in town these individuals, in most cases, also shop while in town. Thus the business places prosper. If the post offices are closed, a portion of the monies usually spent will be lost and the economy of the town suffers.
My constituency extends roughly 200 miles north and south. From the southern end I have also had representations concerning proposed postal closure. Mrs. Ed Rempel, the secretary-treasurer of Plumas, writes:
This idea is very unfavorable. Some people only come to town on Saturdays to do their weekly shopping, pick up the mail and other business.
Our daily papers come through the mail. They are a day late now. This would mean the Friday paper wouldn't be gotten until Monday. Wc the committee of Plumas do not see it as being feasible to close the post office on Saturday.
The mail at present is slow enough coming now. Why delay it more?
My concern is shared by my rural colleagues as well. For example, my neighbour to the west, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), recently sent out a questionnaire. Yorkton-Melville is a rural constituency very much like Dauphin. Cards were sent with the message: "Yes, I am in favour of retaining Saturday postal service in rural communities". Within nine days the hon. member received well over 500 responses stating opposition to the proposed Saturday closing. Over 500 people immediately replied, signing their names to the document. Many signatures represented husbands, wives and families. I thank my colleague for allowing me to bring these responses here tonight to show you, Mr. Speaker.
But Yorkton-Melville is not the only constituency thus affected. Many of my colleagues from other ridings such as Prince Albert, Humboldt-Lake Centre, The Battlefords-Meadow Lake, Kootenay West, Mission-Port Moody, as well as Selkirk-Interlake, have also been concerned and have expressed their concern to me.
In conclusion, I wish to thank the minister again for his response this morning. I commend him for giving a straight answer. May I say that we in this House will be holding him to his words, just as our constituents will who asked us to raise this issue.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post has traditionally played an important role both in the development of this nation's economy and its social fabric, and the Post Office continues to perform a vital role in the every-day lives of all Canadians. For this reason the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet), in answering the question put this morning by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Lewycky), sought to reassure not only the members of this House but also those Canadians living in rural areas that no unilateral decision would be made concerning Saturday delivery on rural routes. The minister clearly said that no such changes would be made without full consultation with those Canadians who would be affected by such a decision.
The Post Office, like any organization, must constantly review its operations if its services are to remain up-to-date. Demographic patterns are changing constantly across Canada. New communities begin and grow rapidly; other communities decline. If the Post Office is to operate efficiently and economically in the best interests of all Canadians, changes in service will have to be made, but we are always cognizant of the fact that all Canadians are entitled to good service wherever they live.
Recently the Post Office has had to adjust to the rapidly escalating costs of energy. The high cost of energy is a reality confronting individual Canadians from coast to coast and it seriously affects the cost of moving the mails.
Governments have been exhorting the Canadian public to practise energy conservation for obvious reasons but mainly because the money we pay for foreign oil has an adverse effect on the nation's economy and our balance of payments. The energy problem affects the pocketbooks of all Canadians and that is one reason why Post Office officials have been considering the possibility of reducing service on 5,000 rural routes, in order to conserve energy. We cannot exhort the Canadian public to conserve energy without attempting to reduce the government's own consumption of energy. Of course, this has to be balanced against the fact that Canadians want to receive the best mail service possible. In fact, the Post Office has been improving service while reducing operating costs. The minister's aim is to ensure that all Canadians, wherever they live, receive adequate service from Canada Post and that while the search for increases in efficiency go on, the service does not decrease.
April 17, 1980
